name: Iterative policy evaluation update

symbols.meaning: new value of s, computed from the old values of its successors

intuition: Use the Bellman equation as an assignment: replace each state's value by the one-step lookahead computed from the current approximation, and repeat.
assumptions: v_0 is arbitrary except that the terminal state, if any, has value 0.
The sequence v_k approaches v_π in the limit whenever v_π itself is guaranteed to exist (γ < 1, or termination from every state).
example: In Example 4.1, one sweep from $v_0 = 0$ gives $v_1(s) = -1$ for every nonterminal state; the second gives $v_2(1) = -1 + \tfrac14(0 - 1 - 1 - 1) = -1.75$.
significance: Each sweep backs up every state once (a full backup). Two arrays implement (4.5) exactly; the in-place variant also converges and usually faster.
pitfalls: Written with v_k on the right, the update is the two-array version; an in-place sweep can use some new values in the same sweep.
Convergence is only in the limit; in practice the loop stops when the largest change falls below θ.

verification.note: The example values are checked by ch04-q002 and ch04.fig4-2-two-array-iterates.

name: Greedy policy improvement

symbols.meaning: value of taking a in s and then following π

intuition: Look one step ahead with $v_\pi$ and pick the action that looks best.
assumptions: Ties may be broken arbitrarily, or shared among the maximizing actions (p. 96).
pitfalls: Improvement needs the model $p(s', r | s, a)$; with only $v_\pi$ and no model it cannot be computed.

name: Value iteration backup

symbols.meaning: the only difference from the policy evaluation backup (4.5)

intuition: One sweep of evaluation with an improvement built in: back up each state with its best action.
assumptions: For arbitrary $v_0$, $v_k \to v_*$ under the conditions that guarantee $v_*$ exists.
pitfalls: Value iteration needs infinitely many sweeps for exact convergence; in practice it stops when the change Δ is small.

name: Bellman optimality equation for v_* (as restated for DP)
tex: v_*(s) = \max_a \mathbb{E}[R_{t+1} + \gamma v_*(S_{t+1}) \mid S_t = s, A_t = a] = \max_a \sum_{s', r} p(s', r|s, a)\big[r + \gamma v_*(s')\big]
intuition: The equation of (3.16)–(3.17), restated as the target that value iteration turns into an update rule.
assumptions: A finite MDP with known dynamics p(s′, r | s, a).
pitfalls: Value iteration (4.10) is this equation with v_k on the right and v_{k+1} on the left.

verification.note: Printed p. 90 (PDF p. 104), checked on the page image.

name: Bellman optimality equation for q_* (as restated for DP)
tex: q_*(s, a) = \mathbb{E}\Big[R_{t+1} + \gamma \max_{a'} q_*(S_{t+1}, a') \,\Big|\, S_t = s, A_t = a\Big] = \sum_{s', r} p(s', r|s, a)\Big[r + \gamma \max_{a'} q_*(s', a')\Big]
intuition: The same idea for action values; it is the target of value iteration on q (Exercise 4.10).
assumptions: A finite MDP with known dynamics.
pitfalls: The max is inside the sum, at the next state.

verification.note: Printed p. 90 (PDF p. 104), checked on the page image.

name: v_π as a one-step expectation
tex: v_\pi(s) = \mathbb{E}_\pi\big[R_{t+1} + \gamma R_{t+2} + \gamma^2 R_{t+3} + \cdots \mid S_t = s\big] = \mathbb{E}_\pi[R_{t+1} + \gamma v_\pi(S_{t+1}) \mid S_t = s]
intuition: A state's value is the expected next reward plus the discounted value of where you land.
assumptions: v_π exists: γ < 1, or termination is guaranteed from every state under π.
pitfalls: Under a policy that can loop for ever with γ = 1, v_π may not exist (Exercise 4.4).

verification.note: Printed p. 90 (PDF p. 104), checked on the page image.

name: Bellman equation for v_π, written out
tex: v_\pi(s) = \sum_a \pi(a|s) \sum_{s', r} p(s', r|s, a)\big[r + \gamma v_\pi(s')\big]

symbols.meaning: probability of a in s under π

intuition: With known dynamics, these are |S| linear equations in |S| unknowns.
pitfalls: A direct linear solve is possible; DP prefers iteration (4.5) because it scales and generalises.

verification.note: Printed p. 90 (PDF p. 104), checked on the page image.

name: Value of trying one action, then following π
tex: q_\pi(s, a) = \mathbb{E}_\pi[R_{t+1} + \gamma v_\pi(S_{t+1}) \mid S_t = s, A_t = a] = \sum_{s', r} p(s', r|s, a)\big[r + \gamma v_\pi(s')\big]

symbols.meaning: the value of taking a in s and following π afterwards

intuition: To decide whether to change π at s, compare this with v_π(s): is one deviation worth it?
assumptions: v_π is known, together with the dynamics.
example: In the 4×4 gridworld under the random policy, from state 1 moving left reaches the terminal state: $q_\pi(1, \text{left}) = -1 + 0 = -1$, far above $v_\pi(1) = -14$.
pitfalls: The first action a need not be π(s); that is the point of the comparison.

verification.note: Printed p. 94 (PDF p. 108), checked on the page image.

name: Condition of the policy improvement theorem

symbols.meaning: the action the new policy takes in s

intuition: In every state, following π′ for one step and then π is at least as good as following π throughout.
assumptions: π and π′ deterministic (the stochastic case uses Σ_a π′(a|s) q_π(s, a))
pitfalls: The condition is about one step of π′; the theorem's conclusion is about following π′ for ever.

verification.note: Printed p. 94 (PDF p. 108), checked on the page image. Checked numerically by ch04.policy-improvement-theorem.

name: Conclusion of the policy improvement theorem

symbols.meaning: the value function of the new policy

intuition: If (4.7) holds everywhere, π′ is at least as good as π everywhere.

derivation.why: (4.7), then (4.6) with the action chosen by π′.
Apply (4.7) again at the next state.
Keep going: every step replaces π by π′ one step further out.

pitfalls: Strict inequality in (4.7) at some state gives strict inequality in (4.8) at some state, not necessarily the same one.

verification.note: Printed p. 94 (PDF p. 108), checked on the page image.

name: One-step value of a stochastic policy

symbols.meaning: probability of a in s under the new policy

intuition: For stochastic policies the theorem uses this average in place of q_π(s, π′(s)).
pitfalls: When several actions tie in (4.9), any split of probability among them is greedy; submaximal actions must get zero.

verification.note: Printed unnumbered on p. 96 (PDF p. 110), checked on the page image.
